title: Mission: a link shortener for enrollment day
subtitle: A viral link, a nosy bot, the whole computer lab on one IP and a public-school budget
mission: The school created a link shortener (lnk.example/…) for everything: enrollment, payment slips, forms. On enrollment day, the form link goes to every parents’ group and the peak reaches 3,000 redirects per second, plus 5 new links per second. A bot tries to guess links from a single IP, 400 times per second. And the whole school shares one internet connection: at peak, 600 requests per minute come from the school’s IP. The intern delivered the cheapest possible design: 1 server, no cache, no replica, sequential ids (1, 2, 3…), no per-IP limit and every click written to the database during the redirect. Fix it until all six criteria turn green. Each server handles 800 requests/s; each database, 900 operations/s; the cache hits 75% of reads.

coach.ui: Move the controls; the criteria change as you adjust. Each failing one says why. The numbers are simulated.
coach.cmd: Edit the command and run it. Each failing criterion says why. Everything you need showed up in lessons 2 to 6.

why.simples:
You designed a real large system, piece by piece. Several servers behind a load balancer, with one spare, so the link doesn’t go down if one burns out. A cache in front of the database, because almost everybody asks for the same link. A replica to split the reads the cache misses. Random ids, so nobody finds other people’s forms by guessing numbers. A per-IP limit that stops the bot without blocking the school. And clicks counted through a queue, out of the way of people who just want to be redirected.
Notice that no piece solved everything on its own: a cache without a replica still leaves the database slow, more servers don’t save a database drowning in clicks, and the cheapest design was the one that cost the most in errors.
why.dev:
The back-of-the-envelope estimate that guides the design: 3,055 requests/s ÷ 800 per server = 3.8 servers at the limit; but latency explodes near 100% utilization (p95 ≈ 3 × service time ÷ (1 − utilization)), so aim for about 65%: 3,055 ÷ (800 × 0.65) ≈ 5.9 → 6 servers, and check N+1 (5 × 800 = 4,000 ≥ 3,055). In the database: without a queue, each click is an UPDATE, 3,000 writes/s on a 900-op database; with the queue batching clicks in groups of 100, they become 30.
Ids: 7 characters from [a-zA-Z0-9] give 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations; draw them with a cryptographic generator and handle collisions with a uniqueness constraint (retry). Per-IP limit: a one-minute window with INCR and EXPIRE in Redis, answering 429 with Retry-After. And the redirect: 302 (or 307) isn’t stored by the browser by default, so every click reaches you; 301 is permanent and can be stored, and then later clicks don’t even pass through the shortener.
why.especialista:
For production there are still missing pieces: the primary database is still a single point of failure (automatic failover, a replica in another zone), the cache needs stampede protection when the viral link expires (a lock or a stale value while refreshing), and a per-IP limit alone is weak against someone using many IPs, so combine it with per-link limits, challenges for suspicious traffic and, for private links, authentication: a hard-to-guess id isn’t access control.
Also think about: a CDN or edge serving the hot link’s redirect, pre-warming before a known event (enrollment day has a date), expiring links, approximate click counts being acceptable (the queue can lag by seconds), bot filtering in the counts, and load tests with the real peak profile before the day. And write the design down with numbers: the assumptions (hit rate, capacity per server) are exactly what changes as the system grows.

success: Mission accomplished! At the enrollment peak, {A} requests/s with a p95 of {p95} ms and {errPct}% errors, for R$ {cost} a month. Losing a server doesn’t take the link down, the bot can’t find anyone’s forms, the school lab isn’t blocked and every click is counted without slowing anyone down. Go ahead and post the link in the parents’ group.

steps: Build the estimate sheet on paper or in a spreadsheet, with these rows: peak requests/s (3,000 + 5 for creation + whatever the bot gets through); capacity per server (800/s); servers = peak ÷ (800 × 0.65), rounded up; N+1 = (servers − 1) × 800 ≥ peak?; database writes with and without batching (3,000 or 3,000 ÷ 100); reads the cache misses (25% of 3,000).

Generate ids the way the shortener would and check the size of the id space:
docker run --rm python:3.14-slim python -c "import secrets, string; a = string.ascii_letters + string.digits; print(''.join(secrets.choice(a) for _ in range(7)))"
docker run --rm python:3.14-slim python -c "print(62**7)"

Try a fixed-window per-IP limit in Redis:
docker run -d --name limite redis:8
docker exec -it limite redis-cli
Inside redis-cli, run these a few times:
INCR limite:203.0.113.7
EXPIRE limite:203.0.113.7 60 NX
TTL limite:203.0.113.7
The counter is this IP’s number of requests in the minute; above the limit, the app answers 429. NX only sets the expiry the first time.
Leave with exit and clean up: docker rm -f limite
recipe.ok: the sheet comes out at 6 servers with N+1 and 30 writes/s with the queue; the first Python command prints a 7-character id of letters and digits that changes every time and the second prints 3521614606208; in Redis, INCR answers 1, 2, 3… and TTL counts down from 60 until the key disappears.
